passage:
Diary, 14th.
Maths test back. I got 11 out of 25. Abhinav got 25, again. He said he didn't even study. Ma'am read out the top marks, and I turned my paper face down fast. Everyone in my row seems to understand fractions except me. Even my handwriting looks messy next to theirs. At home Mummy asked about the test and I said, "Everyone did better than me. I'm just not a maths person." She said, "You're good at other things, Nirmala. My clever girl." I don't feel good at anything tonight. Maybe I'll ask Didi to show me the fraction ones tomorrow.

qa.q: What mark did Nirmala get?
qa.a: She got 11 out of 25.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala turn her paper face down fast?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and behind when the top marks were read out and didn't want anyone to see hers.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do next, and why is that a good step?
qa.a: Ask Didi for help with fractions, as she plans, because it tackles the actual gap instead of the comparison.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt hearing "I'm just not a maths person"?
qa.a: Worried that one test had shaken Nirmala's view of herself, which is why she pointed to her other strengths.

grounding: It shows a girl feeling inferior after comparing her marks and abilities with a classmate's.

passage: Every evening the village children jumped off the rocks into the river, and Ganga, nine like him, swam across and back twice. Thomas couldn't swim. He sat on the bank with his knees pulled up, pretending to watch the fishermen. When a boy called, "Thomas, come in!" he said his stomach hurt. Ganga shouted, "It's easy!" To her it was. He watched her strong arms and felt small and slow, as if everyone had learned something while he wasn't looking. Walking home, he kicked stones and didn't answer when his father asked about his day.

qa.q: How many times did Ganga swim across and back?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why did Thomas say his stomach hurt?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of not being able to swim and wanted an excuse so the others wouldn't find out.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas's father to do?
qa.a: Gently ask about his day again later and, if Thomas shares, offer to teach him or find someone safe to teach him swimming.

qa.q: Why might Ganga's "It's easy!" land badly on Thomas?
qa.a: She meant to encourage him, but because it is easy for her, it made him feel even further behind.

grounding: It shows a village boy feeling small and behind when he compares himself with peers who can swim.

passage: At the athletics trials in Johannesburg, Lindiwe, twelve, ran the 200 metres in her school shoes because her trainers had split. She came fifth. Paulo, who had won every race since Grade 4, finished first without even looking tired, and his parents cheered from the stands. Lindiwe sat on the grass and pulled at her laces. Everyone else seemed to have proper kit, parents watching and a coach's nod. She told herself she would probably never be a real runner. Then Paulo flopped down beside her and said, "Your start was really fast."

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe run in her school shoes?
qa.a: Her trainers had split.

qa.q: What did Lindiwe believe about herself as she pulled at her laces?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and inadequate, believing she would probably never be a real runner because everyone else seemed better equipped and supported.

qa.q: How could a coach respond to Lindiwe after this race?
qa.a: Point out what she did well, like her fast start, and help her find proper shoes through the school if possible.

qa.q: How does Paulo see Lindiwe's race?
qa.a: He noticed her fast start and seems to see her as a real runner, unlike how she sees herself.

grounding: It shows a girl feeling inferior after comparing her kit, support and results with a star runner's.

passage: At the swimming club, Vandana climbed out of the pool, panting. Jasleen had finished two lengths ahead again. The coach said, 'Good try, Vandana,' but only gave Jasleen a high-five. Vandana wrapped herself in her towel and sat on the bench. She looked at Jasleen's strong arms and then her own thin ones. Everyone here is better than me, she thought. I'm the slowest. Why did I even join? When her mother arrived, Vandana said, 'Can I stop swimming?' without looking up.

qa.q: How far ahead did Jasleen finish?
qa.a: Jasleen finished two lengths ahead.

qa.q: What was Vandana thinking as she compared her arms to Jasleen's?
qa.a: She felt inferior and believed everyone was better than her, and doubted she belonged in the club.

qa.q: How could Vandana's mother respond to her question about stopping?
qa.a: She could first ask what happened and listen, then help Vandana compare her times to her own past times instead of to Jasleen.

qa.q: What would change if the coach had given Vandana specific praise too?
qa.a: She might have felt her own progress mattered and been less crushed by the comparison.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling inferior when comparing her abilities to a peer's, at a sports club.

passage: I'm Ishita. My sister Sarika got her Class 6 report card today. I saw her open it at the gate. She got 78 in maths, which is good, I think. But then her friend showed her 96, and Sarika's smile went flat. At home she didn't eat her rice. She kept saying, 'Everyone's smarter than me.' Mummy said 78 was fine. Sarika just shrugged and shut her bedroom door. I don't know if she was angry or sad or both. I left a chocolate outside her door.

qa.q: What mark did Sarika get in maths?
qa.a: She got 78 in maths.

qa.q: What made Sarika's smile go flat?
qa.a: She saw her friend's 96 and felt worse about herself by comparison.

qa.q: What might help Sarika after a day like this?
qa.a: A calm talk later about what she learned and what she can improve, rather than comparing with others, could help.

qa.q: How does Ishita, the narrator, see her sister's mood?
qa.a: Ishita cares about Sarika but is unsure whether she is angry, sad or both, so she shows care with a chocolate.

grounding: Shows a child feeling inferior after comparing her marks with a peer's, described by her sibling.

passage: Monday: Disha, ten, saw Afreen's notebook, neat handwriting, every sum ticked. She hid her own messy book under the desk. Wednesday: when the teacher read out marks, Afreen got nineteen out of twenty. Disha got twelve. She told her mother, "I'm the dumbest in class." Saturday: she asked Afreen how she wrote so neatly. "I copy it again at home," Afreen said. "My first try is messy too." Disha stared, then laughed a little. That night she rewrote one page slowly.

qa.q: What mark did Afreen get?
qa.a: Nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: What does Disha saying "I'm the dumbest in class" suggest?
qa.a: She felt inferior and ashamed when she compared herself with Afreen.

qa.q: What small step helped Disha?
qa.a: Asking Afreen directly, and learning that the neat work came from effort, not magic.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel when Disha asks her?
qa.a: Maybe surprised that anyone envies her and glad to share her secret.

grounding: Shows a child feeling inferior when comparing herself with a classmate, then learning the gap came from effort.

passage: "Payal, you think you're not good enough? At twelve, I, your Ankita Masi, felt the same. My cousin Meena was top of her class, sang at every wedding, and everyone asked her to dance. At family dinners, I sat in the corner, feeling like nothing. One Diwali, Meena's grandmother fell ill, and I was the one who knew her medicines, because I always helped at home. Meena said, 'I could never remember all that.' I realised she wasn't better than me, just different. I still don't sing, though."

qa.q: What was Meena good at?
qa.a: She was top of her class, sang at every wedding, and everyone asked her to dance.

qa.q: How did young Ankita feel at family dinners?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and invisible, sitting in the corner comparing herself with Meena.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Ankita's view?
qa.a: When she knew the grandmother's medicines and Meena admitted she couldn't do that.

qa.q: How might Meena have seen Ankita that Diwali?
qa.a: With new respect, seeing a skill in her she didn't have herself.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling feeling inferior to a cousin as a child and a moment that changed the comparison.

passage: The swimming gala was loud, crowded and running late. Abhinav, eleven, stood in lane four, shivering. On either side were boys who trained every morning. The whistle went. By the second length he could see their feet far ahead. He finished last. In the stands, parents cheered for others. He sat with a towel over his head. His friend Gurleen found him. "You beat your own time," she said, showing him her notebook. "By three seconds." He didn't look up. "Still last." But he took the notebook.

qa.q: Which lane did Abhinav swim in?
qa.a: Lane four.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav sit with a towel over his head?
qa.a: He felt inadequate and embarrassed after finishing last next to boys who trained more.

qa.q: What would you advise Abhinav after the gala?
qa.a: Compare himself with his own past times, like Gurleen did, and keep practising.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurleen to see Abhinav so low?
qa.a: She probably feels concerned and wants to show him his real progress.

grounding: Shows a child feeling inferior to faster peers after a race, with a friend pointing to his own improvement.

passage: In the Pune school, the maths test results were read out. Afreen, 20 out of 20. Aditi, 13. Aditi looked at her desk. On the way home, Afreen chattered about the drawing competition she'd also won. Aditi said nothing. At home she threw her bag down. "I'm the dumbest one," she told her father. "Afreen is good at everything." Her father sat beside her. "Last month you got 9." "But Afreen got 20!" "And you got four more than you did last month." Aditi sniffed. "It still feels small."

qa.q: What did Aditi get on the maths test?
qa.a: 13 out of 20.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she said "I'm the dumbest one"?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and ashamed, comparing herself to Afreen's perfect score.

qa.q: How could her father continue to help Aditi?
qa.a: He could keep pointing to her own progress and help her set a small goal for the next test.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the walk home?
qa.a: Afreen probably didn't notice Aditi was upset, since she was excited about her own wins.

grounding: A girl feels inferior when comparing her maths marks to a friend's perfect score.

passage:
"Deepika, come in! The water's warm!"
"No, I'm fine here."
Devika swam over. "You haven't gone past the rope all summer."
"Everyone else can swim to the other side."
"So can you. Almost."
"I can't. I just splash. You swim like a fish, and even little Riya's faster than me."
"Riya's been going since she was five."
"I'm eleven and I still can't." Deepika wrapped her towel tighter. "Everyone's watching me."
"Nobody's watching. Look, they're all racing."
Deepika glanced up. "Maybe."
"Come to the rope with me. Just the rope."
Deepika hesitated, then stood. "Just the rope."

qa.q: Who swims "like a fish"?
qa.a: Devika.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she wrapped her towel tighter?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and self-conscious, sure everyone was watching her.

qa.q: What small step did Devika suggest?
qa.a: Swimming just to the rope together.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had teased her about not swimming?
qa.a: Deepika would likely feel worse and stay out of the water.

grounding: A girl feels inadequate about her swimming compared with her cousin and others.

passage: I'm Kishore. Last year Indu joined our class from Delhi. The first week, Ma'am asked her to read aloud and she read the English lesson smoothly, like a newsreader. Then it was my turn. I stumbled on "enormous" and "whispered." Someone giggled. My ears went hot. After that, I kept comparing. Indu's handwriting, Indu's answers, Indu's shoes. I felt small all the time. One day Indu asked me to explain a Marathi poem she didn't understand. I did, easily. She said, "You're so good at this." I didn't know what to say.

qa.q: Which words did Kishore stumble on?
qa.a: "Enormous" and "whispered."

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after comparing everything to Indu?
qa.a: Kishore felt small and inadequate all the time.

qa.q: What could Kishore learn from explaining the Marathi poem?
qa.a: That everyone has different strengths, and Kishore has some that Indu admires.

qa.q: How might Indu have seen Kishore during that time?
qa.a: Indu likely saw Kishore as good at Marathi and may not have known Kishore felt small.

grounding: A child looks back on feeling inferior after comparing to a new classmate's English reading.

passage:
Teacher's note, Wednesday.

After the class reading test, Sarita put her head down on the desk. When I asked, she said, "Everyone reads faster than me. I'm the worst."

She had compared her score with three friends. She reads more slowly, but her understanding answers were among the best in class.

I showed her those answers and said reading fast and reading well aren't the same. She sat up a little.

I'll give her a reading buddy and check in weekly.

— Rekha

qa.q: What did Sarita say after the reading test?
qa.a: She said, "Everyone reads faster than me. I'm the worst."

qa.q: How did Sarita feel after comparing her score with her friends?
qa.a: Sarita felt inferior and discouraged, believing she was the worst.

qa.q: How did Rekha help Sarita?
qa.a: Rekha showed her strong answers and explained that reading well matters as much as reading fast.

qa.q: How might Sarita's friends see her reading?
qa.a: They might not realise she felt so bad, since they only compared speed.

grounding: A teacher notes a child feeling inferior after comparing her reading speed with peers, and offers perspective.

passage:
Winter sports day, Friday

Came last in the 100 metres. LAST. Kashish came first, again. Everyone crowded round her.

I stood by the water cooler and felt like the slowest person in the world. Why is she good at everything? Running, maths, drawing. I'm not good at anything.

Then Kashish came over. "You ran really straight. I always wobble." I don't know if she was just being nice.

Mumma says I'm good at looking after the class plants. That's not a sport. But still.

Alka

qa.q: Who came first in the 100 metres?
qa.a: Kashish came first.

qa.q: How did Alka feel after coming last?
qa.a: Alka felt inferior and defeated, like the slowest person in the world.

qa.q: How could Mumma help Alka with this feeling?
qa.a: Mumma could keep noticing Alka's real strengths and remind her that everyone is good at different things.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel coming over to Alka?
qa.a: Kashish may have felt kind and wanted to encourage Alka.

grounding: On winter sports day, a child feels inferior after comparing running times with a talented classmate.

passage:
During the summer holidays, Avni came from Mumbai to the village near Sagar. She spoke English fast, wore shiny sandals, and knew the names of every cricket player.

Vijay, eleven, sat on the charpai in his old rubber slippers. When Avni asked him a question in English, he answered in Hindi and felt his face go hot.

That evening he told his Dadi, "She's better than me at everything."

Dadi said, "Can she milk a buffalo? Can she find the way to the river in the dark?"

Vijay laughed. "No."

"Then teach her tomorrow."

qa.q: What did Avni wear?
qa.a: She wore shiny sandals.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Avni asked him a question in English?
qa.a: Vijay felt embarrassed and inferior, his face going hot.

qa.q: How did Dadi help Vijay?
qa.a: She reminded him of his own skills, like milking a buffalo and finding the way to the river.

qa.q: How might Avni feel if Vijay taught her village skills?
qa.a: Avni might feel excited and impressed, learning new things from him.

grounding: During the summer holidays, a village boy feels inferior comparing himself to his city cousin, and his grandmother helps him see his strengths.

passage: Every Saturday in January the outdoor rink in Toronto was packed. Layla gripped the boards while Vera, from her class, glided backwards and spun twice with her arms tucked in. Their classmates clapped. Layla pushed away from the wall once and landed on her knees. "Everyone here learned when they were three," she mumbled to her cousin Sami, cheeks burning under her scarf. "I'm the worst in the whole class." Sami shrugged. "You've skated for two weeks." Layla watched Vera spin again and pulled her hat low. She didn't take off her skates, though. She pushed away from the boards once more.

qa.q: How many times did Vera spin?
qa.a: Vera spun twice with her arms tucked in.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling when she said she was the worst in the class?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and embarrassed, comparing her two weeks of skating with Vera's easy spins.

qa.q: What could Layla tell herself to make the comparison fairer?
qa.a: She could compare herself with her own first day, not with Vera, and notice how much she has learned in two weeks.

qa.q: How might Vera see Layla at the rink?
qa.a: Vera might not even notice Layla's struggle, or might remember learning slowly too; being judged may feel bigger to Layla than it really is.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling inferior when she compares her new skating with a classmate's skill.
